# Carrier Faithfulness

## What It Measures

Carrier faithfulness is a quality metric for reconstruction data. It asks whether two differently named BEDC carrier classifiers reduce to the same canonical payload. When they do, the carrier layer has not encoded the mathematical distinction that the names claim to mark.

The metric consumes reconstruction pairs already produced by `discovery_production_radar`. It does not run a new structural-DNA pass. A reconstruction pair has the form:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `target` | The later or candidate classifier endpoint |
| `prior` | The earlier classifier endpoint in the same canonical bucket |
| `canonical_payload` | The normalized payload proving that the two endpoints have the same carrier structure |

The audit payload key is `carrier_faithfulness`. It reports `cross_domain_under_encoding_count`, `same_module_sibling_count`, and the list of cross-domain collision pairs with target, prior, domains, and a compact canonical-payload summary.

## Why A Collision Is Evidence

A canonical payload is computed from the normalized carrier expression, not from prose or from the surface name. If two different named concepts have the same canonical payload, then the carrier expression did not encode anything that distinguishes them. The names differ, but the payload says that the formal classifier skeleton is the same.

This is a refutation of faithful encoding for that carrier layer. If the distinguishing mathematics had been encoded into the carrier, the canonical payload would differ. When it does not differ, the distinction is still outside the carrier: in the prose, in the name, in future intended semantics, or nowhere formal.

The metric is therefore not a discovery gate and not a truth oracle. It is a formal quality signal for under-encoding.

## Two Classes

The metric separates reconstruction collisions by the `<X>Up` module or domain segment in the qualified Lean name.

| Class | Reading |
|---|---|
| `same-module sibling` | Target and prior live in the same `Up` module. This can be a weaker problem because sibling variants may intentionally share a carrier skeleton. |
| `cross-domain collision` | Target and prior live in different `Up` domains. This is a strong under-encoding signal: two domain-distinct concepts are represented by the same generic skeleton. |

Same-module siblings are kept visible because excessive internal duplication still matters, but they are not the main signal. Cross-domain collisions are the faithfulness warning: the carrier has become a label pasted onto a reusable skeleton.

## Example

`BEDC.Derived.ContinuousUp.ContinuousModulusWitness` and `BEDC.Derived.CompactUp.CompactNetWitness` collide at the canonical-payload level. Both reduce to a carrier shape built from three `UnaryHistory` witnesses and an append equation.

The mathematical names suggest different domains: continuity/modulus data on one side, compact/net data on the other. The payload does not contain that distinction. Under this metric, that is a cross-domain under-encoding signal.

## Boundary

The metric is informational. It does not change the audit exit code.

Cross-domain collision is a strong signal, not an absolute theorem that the concepts can never be genuinely unified. In rare cases two different names may intentionally converge to one structure. In the current BEDC carrier corpus, however, distinct domain names colliding through canonical payload equality should be read as under-encoding unless the carrier has an explicit formal reason for the identification.

The target is not cosmetic differentiation. Adding irrelevant fields, tags, or wrappers merely to change the payload would be gaming the metric. The intended improvement is to encode the distinguishing mathematics: the structure that makes a modulus witness a modulus witness, a compact net a compact net, and so on.

Over time, the quality objective is to reduce `cross_domain_under_encoding_count` by making carriers faithful, not by hiding collisions.
